description: Is TF healthy, and what is slow. Provisioned from docker/observability/dashboards/ — edits made here cannot be saved back.

panels.description: Fixed TraceQL against Tempo. These are searches, not aggregates: each row is one trace, and opening it is the whole point of the row.
panels.title: Traces — what just happened

panels.description: One row per org's GitHub poll cycle. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall. Duration is the whole org's refresh + diff + emit; the waterfall says which repo batch spent it. An empty list means no org polled GitHub in the window — which for an org that tracks no repos is the correct answer, not a fault.
panels.title: GitHub poll cycles

panels.description: One row per org's Jira poll cycle. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall.
panels.title: Jira poll cycles

panels.description: Scorer, repo profiler, and project classifier cycles. All three share this span name — open a row and read the `job` attribute to see which. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall.
panels.title: System job cycles

panels.description: Every verb, not just reads — the mutating routes are where the slow work usually is (writes, delegation dispatch). Server spans are named "<METHOD> <route pattern>", never the concrete path, so no repo name or other tenant data reaches this list. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall. The DB spans underneath usually explain the time. Empty is the healthy state.
panels.title: API requests slower than 500 ms

panels.description: Every span that ended with an error status, any subsystem. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall. Anticipated skips (provider backoff, dedup, quiet-skip) are recorded as an `outcome` attribute rather than an error status, so this list stays things that are actually wrong.
panels.title: Errored spans

panels.description: Derived from the spans above by Tempo's metrics generator (traces_spanmetrics_*) and remote-written to Prometheus. Covers every instrumented subsystem at once, so it grows on its own as new span families land.
panels.title: RED — rate, errors, duration by span name

panels.description: Calls per second for every span name Tempo has seen. The legend is sorted by peak, so the busiest paths are at the top.
panels.title: Request rate by span name

panels.description: Share of calls that ended with an error status. Span names with no errors are absent rather than plotted at zero, so 'No data' here means nothing errored and anything drawn is worth a look.
panels.title: Error rate by span name

panels.description: Click an exemplar dot to open the trace behind that sample — the metrics→traces bridge, and the fastest route from 'the p95 moved' to the one request that moved it.
panels.title: p95 latency by span name

panels.description: Scraped from each pod's :9464. Every series here is per-process: in a scaled fleet the pods are separate lines, told apart by tf_service (control vs executor).
panels.title: Runtime — the pod itself

panels.description: Multi mode holds two pools per pod that behave nothing alike — `admin` serves the JWT-less background jobs, `app` serves RLS-bound request handlers. Local mode has one, named `local`. A max of 0 means unlimited.
panels.title: DB pool connections

panels.description: Time spent blocked waiting for a connection, per second of wall clock. This is the saturation signal the connection counts can't give you: a request waiting on the pool hasn't started a statement yet, so it looks exactly like a fast query until it shows up here. Flat zero is the healthy shape.
panels.title: DB pool contention

panels.description: TF's own server histogram, independent of the trace pipeline — this panel keeps working with tracing switched off. Routes are ServeMux patterns, so no concrete path (and no repo name) reaches the label.
panels.title: HTTP requests by response status

panels.description: A number that only ever climbs is the signature of a leaked goroutine — a poll cycle or run that starts one per iteration and never returns.
panels.title: Goroutines

panels.description: RSS as the kernel sees it. In multi mode the executor's dispatch admission gate is driven by host memory headroom, so this is the number that decides whether a run is allowed to start.
panels.title: Resident memory

panels.description: Empty unless a Slack app is connected. Sustained retries are the precursor to Slack disabling the app's event subscription, and app_rate_limited means Slack is dropping deliveries at the source — those are never retried.
panels.title: Slack ingest

panels.description: The router's spans. One `route.event` root per durable-queue row, linked back to the `event.enqueue` that produced it rather than parented to it — a poll cycle emits many events and they route later, possibly on another pod. All three empty means nothing routed in the window, which for a deployment tracking no repos or projects is the correct answer, not a fault.
panels.title: Event pipeline — what routing did with each event

panels.description: One row per queue row the router claimed, sorted by the wait rather than by recency. `queue.wait_ms` is the enqueue→claim interval — over before this span starts, so nothing else in the trace can show it, and without it a backed-up queue and slow routing look identical. `disposition` is what routing decided: most values end the pipeline early (`frozen`, the three `taskless_*`), so a pass that did nothing looks like a fast span until you read the column, and `error` is a disposition rather than a span error status — the store call that failed carries the status on its own span, where the cause is. Click a Span ID to open the routing trace; the filter icon keeps one disposition. Empty means nothing routed in the window.
panels.title: Routed events — queue wait and disposition

panels.description: `route.event` and `route.delegate` call rates, per minute. The delegation line is the operator-visible consequence of a trigger's configuration — enable a prompt_trigger and this is where it moves, and there is nowhere else it shows. The `conversation.id` each delegation started is an attribute on the `route.delegate` span, reached by opening that event's trace. A flat zero delegation line under a live routing line is the ordinary shape where no auto-delegation is configured.
panels.title: Events routed and delegations started

panels.description: p95 by stage. `route.event` is the whole pass; the rest are its children — inline close checks, task_rule matching, team routing, the task upsert, trigger predicates, and the spawn enqueue. Read with the queue wait to the left, this says which half is slow: a short wait with a slow stage is slow routing, a long wait with fast stages is a backed-up queue. A stage with no calls in the window is absent rather than drawn at zero.
panels.title: Routing stage latency (p95)

panels.description: One `engagement.setup` root per claim attempt, from the claim to agent-live. What follows agent-live is punctual spans linked back to it rather than children, because a span exports only once it ends and the streaming period is unbounded. Local mode takes a shorter path — no broker, sidecar, or credential spans exist there at all — and their absence is the path not taken, never a fault.
panels.title: Delegated runs — engagement setup

panels.description: One row per claim attempt, most recent first; `Duration` is the whole setup, claim to agent-live. `outcome` is the closed set — `agent_live` reached the agent, `cancelled` was stopped by someone, `shutdown` stood down for its departing executor and left the claim for the boot reconcile, `fenced` lost the conversation to a successor, `no_message` had nothing to deliver, `not_started` is an exit that did not say why, and `setup_failed` is the only one that also carries an error status. An error rate over engagements therefore has to read this attribute rather than the span status, or every stopped run counts as a failure. A requeued run is one row per attempt, sharing `conversation.id` and told apart by `claim.attempt`. Click a Span ID for the setup waterfall; empty means nothing was claimed in the window.
panels.title: Engagement setups — outcome and attempt

panels.description: Mean wall clock per call for each setup phase: the fleet-level answer to "why did that run take four minutes to start". For one specific run, open its trace from the table to the left instead. The phases NEST — `engagement.sandbox.bringup` contains the `sandbox.*` and `sidecar.*` children — so the lines deliberately do not stack and do not sum to the root. The credential park that also sits inside bring-up has its own panel below, since it measures another pod's work rather than this one's. In local mode the sandbox, sidecar and jail phases have no calls and are simply absent, leaving fetch, clone, staging and the SDK install.
panels.title: Setup phase breakdown — mean duration

panels.description: p95 of the two halves of credential provisioning, which are two traces on purpose: `engagement.credentials.await` is the executor parked in `awaiting_credentials`, `credentials.provision` is the control pod sealing a bundle to that run's sidecar key. They are deliberately not linked — the doorbell between them is lossy by design and the sweep is the real completion path, so a link would promise a handoff neither side can guarantee. Both carry `conversation.id`, which is the join for one run: search it in Explore. A park much longer than the seal means the doorbell was missed and the sweep collected it; the `count` attribute on the await span is the poll count that says which. Both are empty in local mode, which has no sidecar to seal to.
panels.title: Credential wait — the park and the seal

panels.description: One row per privileged host operation the executor asked the cap-broker to perform, slowest first; `Duration` is the round trip as the caller experienced it. The broker exports no spans of its own — permanently, so the most privileged process on the host gains no outbound network dependency — which makes these client-side spans the only record its work has anywhere. `op` is the broker method, a Go constant from the dispatching switch: filter it to compare `SetupNetwork` against `LaunchRun` against a teardown. Teardown calls land in their run's trace after the setup root ended, so a trace legitimately reads setup, gap, tail. Empty in local mode: there is no broker there.
panels.title: Broker IPC calls by op
